name: Nodular regenerative hyperplasia of the liver

reference.source: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System / EASL vascular liver disease guidance
clinicalPearls: A leading cause of non-cirrhotic portal hypertension, presenting with varices, splenomegaly or ascites while synthetic liver function is often preserved
Characterised histologically by diffuse micronodular transformation of hepatocytes without the fibrous septa of true cirrhosis
Strongly associated with systemic disease including autoimmune and connective-tissue disorders, myeloproliferative and lymphoproliferative conditions, and HIV
Frequently linked to drugs and toxins, notably thiopurines, oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy and certain antiretrovirals
Liver enzymes may be near-normal or show a mild cholestatic pattern, so a normal biochemistry does not exclude the diagnosis
Reticulin staining on an adequate biopsy is often needed, as routine imaging and standard histology can miss the subtle nodularity
Management targets portal-hypertensive complications and, where possible, the underlying cause or offending drug
reference.pathophysiology: Nodular regenerative hyperplasia is thought to result from heterogeneous hepatic blood flow: obliteration or injury of small portal venules leads to atrophy of poorly perfused acini and compensatory hyperplasia of well-perfused hepatocytes. This produces diffuse regenerative micronodules unaccompanied by significant fibrosis. The altered intrahepatic vascular resistance and obliterative portal venopathy generate presinusoidal portal hypertension while hepatocellular function is relatively spared, distinguishing it from cirrhosis.
additionalDifferentials: Idiopathic non-cirrhotic portal hypertension / porto-sinusoidal vascular disease
additionalInvestigations: Liver biopsy with reticulin staining to demonstrate micronodular architecture without bridging fibrosis
Cross-sectional imaging to exclude cirrhosis and macroscopic focal lesions
Hepatic venous pressure gradient and portal-system imaging to characterise portal hypertension
Screening for associated autoimmune, myeloproliferative and lymphoproliferative disorders
Medication and toxin history including thiopurines and chemotherapy exposure
Upper endoscopy to assess for varices
redFlags: Progressive ascites or refractory portal-hypertensive complications
Features suggesting an underlying occult malignancy or myeloproliferative disorder
Rapid deterioration raising the possibility of superimposed vascular thrombosis
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally more favourable than cirrhosis because hepatocellular function is preserved, and outcome is largely determined by control of portal-hypertensive complications and the course of any associated systemic disease.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the condition as cirrhosis and mislabelling the patient's prognosis and management
Excluding it on the basis of normal liver enzymes or unremarkable imaging
Failing to request reticulin staining, without which the diagnosis is easily missed
Overlooking a causative drug or associated systemic disorder that should be addressed
references: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System
EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines on vascular diseases of the liver
